questions.stem: Consider concurrent execution of two transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$ in a DBMS, both of which access a data object $A$. For these two transactions to not conflict on $A$, which one of the following statements must be true?

steps.title: What it means for operations to conflict
steps.body: A transaction is a sequence of reads and writes on data items. Two operations **conflict** when all three hold: they belong to different transactions, they touch the same item, and at least one of them is a write. Conflict matters because the order of two conflicting operations changes what a transaction reads or what value is finally stored, while two reads in either order change nothing.

steps.title: Apply the rule to the four combinations on $A$
steps.body: Both read: no write, so no conflict. $T_1$ reads and $T_2$ writes: read-write conflict. $T_1$ writes and $T_2$ reads: write-read conflict. Both write: write-write conflict. Only the first pair avoids a conflict.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The two transactions do not conflict on $A$ only when both merely read it, which is option A.

shortcut.body: The only conflict-free pair on one item is read-read. Pick the option with no write in it, about 20 seconds.

traps.text: Thinking a reader is harmless to a writer. If $T_2$ writes before $T_1$ reads, $T_1$ sees the new value; if after, the old one, so the order matters and the pair conflicts.
The mirror image of option B: $T_2$ may read the value before or after $T_1$ writes it, which is exactly a write-read conflict.
Assuming that two writes of the same item commute. The last writer decides the final value, so swapping them changes the database.

recognize.clues: The words "do not conflict" and a single shared item $A$ with each transaction either reading or writing it point to the read and write test on one item.
recognize.contrast: Conflict serializability asks whether a whole schedule can be reordered to a serial one. Here only the pairwise test is needed, with no precedence graph.

check.body: Test the opposite case by swapping. If both only read $A$, either order gives each transaction the same value, so the swap is harmless. If either writes $A$, a swap changes a value some transaction sees or the final value, so the pair does conflict.

questions.stem:
An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account $A$ attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. 10000 each from account $A$ to account $B$. Both transactions read the same value, Rs. 11000, as the initial balance in $A$ and were allowed to go through. $B$ was credited Rs. 10000 twice. $A$ was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. 1000.

Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system?

steps.title: The four ACID properties in plain words
steps.body: **Atomicity**: a transaction happens completely or not at all. **Consistency**: a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state, where valid means it obeys the rules (here, money is neither created nor destroyed). **Isolation**: concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one after the other. **Durability**: once a transaction commits, its effects survive a crash.

steps.title: What happened in the story
steps.body: Both transfers read the balance 11000 before either wrote. Each then wrote $11000-10000=1000$ to $A$ (a lost update) and added 10000 to $B$. Total money rose by 10000, since $B$ gained 20000 and $A$ lost only 10000.

steps.title: Check each property
steps.body: Isolation is violated: the result matches neither serial order (serially the second transfer would see 1000 and be refused or overdraw). Consistency is violated: the total is no longer conserved, so the final state is invalid. Atomicity is not shown to be violated: each transfer did all its steps, nothing was half done. Durability is not involved: no committed work was lost in a crash.

shortcut.body: A lost update from two interleaved readers is always an isolation failure, and since money appeared from nowhere the invariant broke, so consistency fails with it. No crash or half-done transaction is mentioned, so rule out atomicity and durability. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Calling it atomicity because only half the money moved. Each transaction did every step it intended; the damage came from interleaving, not from an unfinished transaction.
Durability concerns committed data being lost after a crash. No crash is part of the story.
Choosing isolation alone. The question asks for properties certain to be violated, and a state that creates money also breaks consistency.

recognize.clues: Two transfers that both read the same balance, 11000, before either wrote point to a lost update. The money total changing (B gains 20000 while A loses 10000) shows a broken rule, which points to consistency.
recognize.contrast: Atomicity looks similar because the final state is wrong, but it needs a transaction left half done, usually by a crash. Here each transfer ran every step; the damage came from two transactions running at once.

check.body: Moving money from $A$ to $B$ should leave $A+B$ unchanged. Before, the total is $11000+B$. After, it is $1000+(B+20000)=B+21000$, which is 10000 too much, so consistency broke. In a serial order the second transfer would see $A=1000$ and be refused or overdraw, so $B$ could gain 10000 at most; the interleaved result matches neither serial order, so isolation broke.

questions.stem: Consider the database transactions T1 and T2, and data items X and Y. Which of the schedule(s) is/are conflict serializable?
options: R1(X), W2(X), W1(Y), W2(Y), R1(X), W1(X), COMMIT(T2), COMMIT(T1)
W2(X), R1(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), COMMIT(T1)
R1(X), W1(Y), W2(X), W2(Y), R1(X), W1(X), COMMIT(T1), COMMIT(T2)
W2(X), R1(X), W1(Y), W2(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), COMMIT(T1)

solutionDiagram.alt: Four small precedence graphs for options A to D; only option B is acyclic, with the single direction T2 to T1.

steps.title: Conflict serializability in plain words
steps.body: A **schedule** is one interleaving of the operations of several transactions, each transaction keeping its own order. Two operations **conflict** when they come from different transactions, touch the same data item, and at least one is a write: read-write, write-read and write-write. Swapping two adjacent operations that do not conflict changes nothing; swapping two that conflict can change what a transaction reads or what the database ends up holding. Two schedules are **conflict equivalent** when every conflicting pair appears in the same order in both. The **precedence graph** has one node per transaction and an edge $T_i \to T_j$ whenever an operation of $T_i$ conflicts with and comes before an operation of $T_j$. A schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this graph has no cycle, and any topological order of the graph is an equivalent serial schedule.

steps.title: List the conflicting pairs
steps.body: Both items are written by T2, and T1 reads or writes them, so both X and Y can create edges. T1 reads X twice, writes X once and writes Y once; T2 writes X and writes Y. Commits never conflict. A cycle needs one pair that points $T_1 \to T_2$ and another that points $T_2 \to T_1$.

steps.title: Build the graph of each option
steps.body: A: R1(X) before W2(X) gives $T_1\to T_2$; W2(X) before the second R1(X) gives $T_2\to T_1$. Cycle. B: W2(X) before R1(X), W2(Y) before W1(Y), and W2(X) before W1(X): every edge is $T_2\to T_1$. No cycle. C: R1(X) before W2(X) gives $T_1\to T_2$ on X, and W1(Y) before W2(Y) gives $T_1\to T_2$ on Y, while W2(X) before the second R1(X) gives $T_2\to T_1$ on X. Cycle. D: W2(X) before R1(X) gives $T_2\to T_1$, while W1(Y) before W2(Y) gives $T_1\to T_2$. Cycle.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only option B has an acyclic graph; it is equivalent to the serial schedule $T_2$ then $T_1$.

shortcut.body: Look at the first operation on X in each option. Whenever R1(X) comes before W2(X) and a later R1(X) comes after it, T1 straddles T2 and a cycle exists. Options A and C do exactly that. D splits X and Y in opposite directions. B keeps all T2 operations before T1 on both items. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Reading only the order of the commits (T2 commits first) and assuming that gives T2 then T1. Conflicts are decided by the data operations, and R1(X) precedes W2(X) here.
Option C commits T1 first and looks tidy, but R1(X) sits on both sides of W2(X), so the graph has the cycle $T_1\leftrightarrow T_2$.
It resembles B on X but swaps the order on Y: W1(Y) comes before W2(Y), giving $T_1\to T_2$ against $T_2\to T_1$ on X.

recognize.clues: The phrase "conflict serializable" with operations listed in order for two transactions on two items points to building a precedence graph and testing it for a cycle.
recognize.contrast: View serializability also compares reads-from relations and final writes. The question names conflicts, so only the order of conflicting pairs matters.

check.body: For B, the pairs are $W_2(X)$ before $R_1(X)$, $W_2(X)$ before $W_1(X)$ and $W_2(Y)$ before $W_1(Y)$. All put $T_2$ first, so the serial order $T_2$ then $T_1$ keeps every pair. For A and C, $R_1(X)$ before $W_2(X)$ needs $T_1$ first while $W_2(X)$ before the second $R_1(X)$ needs $T_2$ first. For D, $W_2(X)$ before $R_1(X)$ needs $T_2$ first while $W_1(Y)$ before $W_2(Y)$ needs $T_1$ first. No serial order satisfies opposing pairs.

questions.stem:
A schedule of three database transactions $T_1$, $T_2$, and $T_3$ is shown. $R_i(A)$ and $W_i(A)$ denote read and write of data item $A$ by transaction $T_i$, $i = 1,2,3$. The transaction $T_1$ aborts at the end. Which other transaction(s) will be required to be rolled back?

$R_1(X)\ W_1(Y)\ R_2(X)\ R_2(Y)\ R_3(Y)\ ABORT(T_1)$

solutionDiagram.alt: Three columns of operations. Arrows from W1(Y) to R2(Y) and to R3(Y) mark dirty reads; T1 aborts at the bottom.

steps.title: Abort, dirty read and cascading rollback
steps.body: When a transaction aborts, all its writes are undone. A **dirty read** is a read of a value written by a transaction that has not yet committed. If $T_j$ read a value written by $T_i$ and $T_i$ aborts, the value $T_j$ used never officially existed, so $T_j$ must also roll back, and then so must anyone who read from $T_j$. This chain is a **cascading rollback**.

steps.title: Find who read what $T_1$ wrote
steps.body: $T_1$ writes only $Y$, with $W_1(Y)$, and has not committed when it aborts. $R_2(X)$ reads $X$, which $T_1$ only read, so it is harmless. $R_2(Y)$ reads $Y$ after $W_1(Y)$: a dirty read, so $T_2$ rolls back. $R_3(Y)$ also reads $Y$ after $W_1(Y)$: another dirty read, so $T_3$ rolls back.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Both $T_2$ and $T_3$ must be rolled back, option C.

shortcut.body: Scan after the write of the aborting transaction and list every transaction that reads that item: here Y is read by T2 and T3. Reads of items the aborting transaction never wrote (X) do not count. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Stopping at T2 because it appears first and also reads X. T3 reads Y too, and being later in the schedule does not protect it.
Counting only the last reader. Both $R_2(Y)$ and $R_3(Y)$ follow $W_1(Y)$, so T2 is included.
Assuming only committed transactions are affected by an abort. T2 and T3 had not committed and they used uncommitted data, which is precisely what forces the rollback.

recognize.clues: An abort at the end of the schedule and the question about which other transactions must roll back point to dirty reads and the cascade they cause.
recognize.contrast: Recoverability only constrains the order of commits. Here nothing has committed, so the question is who must be undone, which is the cascading rollback.

check.body: Delete $W_1(Y)$ from the schedule and see what changes. $R_2(Y)$ and $R_3(Y)$ would read the earlier value of $Y$, so their results depend on $T_1$. $R_2(X)$ would read the same $X$ as before, so it does not. Only the readers of $Y$ relied on the aborted write.

questions.stem: Once the DBMS informs the user that a transaction has been successfully completed, its effect should persist even if the system crashes before all its changes are reflected on disk. This property is called

steps.title: The four ACID properties
steps.body: **Atomicity**: all of a transaction or none of it. **Consistency**: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. **Isolation**: concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work. **Durability**: after the DBMS reports commit, the effects remain even if the system crashes.

steps.title: Match the sentence
steps.body: The sentence speaks of the user having been told the transaction completed and of a crash afterwards, with changes not yet on disk. The DBMS keeps this promise by writing the log to stable storage before reporting commit and redoing from it on restart. A promise about surviving a crash after commit is durability.

shortcut.body: The words "persist even if the system crashes" name durability directly. Ten seconds.

traps.text: Atomicity also involves crashes, but it is about a transaction that had not finished: it is undone entirely. Here the transaction already completed.
Consistency is about rules such as keys and balances holding, not about surviving crashes.
Isolation concerns concurrent transactions seeing each other, and no concurrency is mentioned.

recognize.clues: The words "persist" and "crashes" in the sentence, with the user already told of success, name the promise about surviving a crash after commit.
recognize.contrast: Atomicity also speaks of crashes, but about a transaction that had not finished. Durability applies after the DBMS has reported completion.

check.body: Test each property against the sentence by changing the story. If the crash came before the commit message, the requirement would be undoing the work, which is atomicity. Because the sentence puts the crash after the success message, the work must be kept, which separates the two.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the Two Phase Locking (2PL) protocol is/are TRUE?
options: With 2PL, a transaction always locks the data item being read or written just before every operation and always releases the lock just after the operation
With 2PL, once a lock is released on any data item inside a transaction, no more locks on any data item can be obtained inside that transaction

steps.title: What 2PL says
steps.body: A **lock** lets one transaction use a data item while others wait. In **two-phase locking** every transaction has a growing phase, where it only acquires locks, followed by a shrinking phase, where it only releases them. The rule: once a transaction releases any lock it may never acquire another. The point where it holds all its locks is the **lock point**.

steps.title: Judge each statement
steps.body: A is true: ordering transactions by their lock points gives an equivalent serial order, so every 2PL schedule is conflict serializable. B is false: locking just before and releasing just after each operation would release a lock before later locks are taken, which breaks the two-phase rule. C is the definition of 2PL, true. D is true: 2PL does not order the lock requests, so $T_1$ holding $X$ and wanting $Y$ while $T_2$ holds $Y$ and wants $X$ is a deadlock.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: A, C and D are true.

shortcut.body: Recall the three facts about plain 2PL: ensures serializability, no lock after the first unlock, can deadlock. B describes the opposite of two-phase behaviour. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Marking B as true because it sounds like careful locking. Releasing right after each operation is the shrinking phase starting immediately, so no further lock may be taken, and the protocol would not be 2PL.
Dropping D because 2PL "guarantees serializability". Serializability and deadlock freedom are separate: only conservative 2PL avoids deadlock.
Doubting A because 2PL schedules may be non-recoverable. The statement concerns serializability, which always holds.

recognize.clues: The name "Two Phase Locking" and statements about when locks are taken and released, about serializability and about deadlock all point to the basic properties of the protocol.
recognize.contrast: Strict and conservative 2PL add extra rules, such as holding exclusive locks to commit or taking all locks at the start. Basic 2PL has neither, so it can still deadlock.

check.body: Test the deadlock claim by a concrete schedule. Let $T_1$ lock $X$ and $T_2$ lock $Y$, then let each request the other item. Both follow the two-phase rule and each waits for the other forever, so deadlock is possible. Test the lock-after-unlock claim by noting that a transaction that locked after unlocking would have a second growing phase.

$S$: $r_1(z); w_1(z); r_2(x); r_3(y); w_3(y); r_2(y); w_2(x); w_2(y);$

solutionDiagram.alt: Precedence graph with T1 isolated and one edge from T3 to T2 on item y.

steps.body: A **schedule** is one interleaving of the operations of several transactions, each transaction keeping its own order. questions.stem:
Let $R_i(z)$ and $W_i(z)$ denote read and write operations on a data element $z$ by a transaction $T_i$, respectively. Consider the schedule $S$ with four transactions.

$S$: $R_4(x)\,R_2(x)\,R_3(x)\,R_1(y)\,W_1(y)\,W_2(x)\,W_3(y)\,R_4(y)$

Which one of the following serial schedules is conflict equivalent to $S$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Precedence graph on T1, T3, T4, T2 with edges T1 to T3, T1 to T4, T3 to T4 on y and T3 to T2, T4 to T2 on x.

steps.title: Conflict equivalence in plain words
steps.body: A **schedule** is one interleaving of the operations of several transactions, each transaction keeping its own order. Two operations **conflict** when they come from different transactions, touch the same data item, and at least one is a write: read-write, write-read and write-write. Swapping two adjacent operations that do not conflict changes nothing; swapping two that conflict can change what a transaction reads or what the database ends up holding. Two schedules are **conflict equivalent** when every conflicting pair appears in the same order in both. The **precedence graph** has one node per transaction and an edge $T_i \to T_j$ whenever an operation of $T_i$ conflicts with and comes before an operation of $T_j$. A schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this graph has no cycle, and any topological order of the graph is an equivalent serial schedule.

steps.title: Edges from item $x$
steps.body: On $x$ the order is $R_4, R_2, R_3, W_2$. The reads do not conflict with each other. Each read by another transaction before $W_2(x)$ gives an edge into $T_2$: $T_4\to T_2$ and $T_3\to T_2$.

steps.title: Edges from item $y$
steps.body: On $y$ the order is $R_1, W_1, W_3, R_4$. $T_1$ comes before $T_3$ (read-write and write-write): $T_1\to T_3$. $W_1(y)$ before $R_4(y)$: $T_1\to T_4$. $W_3(y)$ before $R_4(y)$: $T_3\to T_4$.

steps.title: Order and answer
steps.body: The edges are $T_1\to T_3$, $T_1\to T_4$, $T_3\to T_4$, $T_3\to T_2$, $T_4\to T_2$. There is no cycle. $T_1$ has no incoming edge so it is first; then only $T_3$ is free; then $T_4$; then $T_2$. The only order is $T_1,T_3,T_4,T_2$, option A.

shortcut.body: Check each option against two edges only: T3 before T4 (W3(y) then R4(y)) kills B and C, and T1 before T3 (W1(y) then W3(y)) kills D. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Putting $T_4$ before $T_3$ because $R_4(x)$ appears first. The conflict on y is $W_3(y)$ before $R_4(y)$, so $T_3$ must precede $T_4$.
Starting with $T_4$ because its first operation heads the schedule. $T_4$ also reads $y$ after $T_1$ and $T_3$ wrote it, so it cannot be first.
Putting $T_3$ ahead of $T_1$. On y, $R_1(y)W_1(y)$ come before $W_3(y)$, which forces $T_1\to T_3$.

recognize.clues: A schedule over four transactions with a question about which serial schedule is conflict equivalent points to a precedence graph and a topological order.
recognize.contrast: Checking only the first operations or the commit order is not enough. Equivalence is decided by conflicting pairs on each item.

check.body: Take the serial order $T_1T_3T_4T_2$ and rebuild it from $S$ by moving only non-conflicting operations. On $y$ the order $R_1,W_1,W_3,R_4$ is the same in both. On $x$ the serial order has $R_3,R_4,R_2,W_2$; only reads moved, and $W_2(x)$ is still after every read, as in $S$. So every conflicting pair keeps its order and the schedules are conflict equivalent.

questions.stem:
Let $S$ be the following schedule of operations of three transactions $T_1$, $T_2$ and $T_3$ in a relational database system:

$R_2(Y), R_1(X), R_3(Z), R_1(Y), W_1(X), R_2(Z), W_2(Y), R_3(X), W_3(Z)$

Consider the statements P and Q below:

P: $S$ is conflict-serializable.
Q: If $T_3$ commits before $T_1$ finishes, then $S$ is recoverable.

Which one of the following choices is correct?
options: Both P and Q are true.
P is true and Q is false.
P is false and Q is true.
Both P and Q are false.

solutionDiagram.alt: Precedence graph: T1 to T2 on Y, T2 to T3 on Z, T1 to T3 on X. No cycle.

steps.title: The two ideas: conflict serializable and recoverable
steps.body: A **schedule** is one interleaving of the operations of several transactions, each transaction keeping its own order. Two operations **conflict** when they come from different transactions, touch the same data item, and at least one is a write: read-write, write-read and write-write. Swapping two adjacent operations that do not conflict changes nothing; swapping two that conflict can change what a transaction reads or what the database ends up holding. Two schedules are **conflict equivalent** when every conflicting pair appears in the same order in both. The **precedence graph** has one node per transaction and an edge $T_i \to T_j$ whenever an operation of $T_i$ conflicts with and comes before an operation of $T_j$. A schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this graph has no cycle, and any topological order of the graph is an equivalent serial schedule. A schedule is **recoverable** when every transaction commits only after every transaction whose written value it has read has committed. Otherwise, if the writer aborted, the reader would have used a value that never became real and could not be undone.

steps.title: Statement P
steps.body: Conflicts in order: on Y, $R_1(Y)$ before $W_2(Y)$ gives $T_1\to T_2$ ($R_2(Y)$ first is read-read). On Z, $R_2(Z)$ before $W_3(Z)$ gives $T_2\to T_3$, and $R_3(Z)$ before $W_3(Z)$ is the same transaction. On X, $W_1(X)$ before $R_3(X)$ gives $T_1\to T_3$ ($R_1(X)$ before is its own). Edges: $T_1\to T_2$, $T_2\to T_3$, $T_1\to T_3$. No cycle, so P is true (equivalent to $T_1T_2T_3$).

steps.title: Statement Q
steps.body: $T_3$ executes $R_3(X)$ after $W_1(X)$, so $T_3$ read a value written by $T_1$. For recoverability $T_1$ must commit before $T_3$. Q says $T_3$ commits before $T_1$ finishes, which is the forbidden order, so $S$ would not be recoverable. Q is false.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: P true, Q false: option B.

shortcut.body: Draw three edges from the first conflicting pair on each item, find no cycle, then spot T3 reading T1's X write: a reader committing before the writer is the textbook non-recoverable case. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Marking Q true by reading it as "all transactions commit eventually". The statement fixes T3 committing before T1 finishes, with T3 having read T1's write.
Thinking a cycle exists because Y and Z are shared by T2 with two different transactions. All three edges go forward in the order T1, T2, T3.
Adding a false edge such as $T_3\to T_1$ from $R_3(Z)$ before something. $T_1$ never touches Z, so no edge arises there.

recognize.clues: Statement Q fixes a commit order ("$T_3$ commits before $T_1$ finishes") and asks whether the schedule is recoverable, so the reads-from pairs matter. Statement P about a cycle is the precedence-graph test on the same schedule.
recognize.contrast: Conflict serializability looks only at the order of operations and ignores commits. Recoverability looks only at who read whose write and who committed first. A schedule can pass one test and fail the other.

check.body: Test P by building the serial schedule $T_1T_2T_3$ and comparing each conflicting pair: $R_1(Y)$ before $W_2(Y)$, $R_2(Z)$ before $W_3(Z)$ and $W_1(X)$ before $R_3(X)$ all keep their order. Test Q by imagining $T_1$ aborting after $W_1(X)$: $T_3$ has already read that value, and if $T_3$ has committed it cannot be undone.

Let $r_i(z)$ and $w_i(z)$ denote read and write operations respectively on a data item $z$ by a transaction $T_i$. Consider the following two schedules.

$S_1$: $r_1(x)\,r_1(y)\,r_2(x)\,r_2(y)\,w_2(y)\,w_1(x)$
$S_2$: $r_1(x)\,r_2(x)\,r_2(y)\,w_2(y)\,r_1(y)\,w_1(x)$

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: $S_1$ is conflict serializable, and $S_2$ is not conflict serializable.
$S_1$ is not conflict serializable, and $S_2$ is conflict serializable.

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: precedence graph of S1 with edges T1 to T2 on y and T2 to T1 on x, a cycle. Right: S2 with only T2 to T1.

steps.title: The test for conflict serializability
steps.body: A **schedule** is one interleaving of the operations of several transactions, each transaction keeping its own order. Two operations **conflict** when they come from different transactions, touch the same data item, and at least one is a write: read-write, write-read and write-write. Swapping two adjacent operations that do not conflict changes nothing; swapping two that conflict can change what a transaction reads or what the database ends up holding. Two schedules are **conflict equivalent** when every conflicting pair appears in the same order in both. The **precedence graph** has one node per transaction and an edge $T_i \to T_j$ whenever an operation of $T_i$ conflicts with and comes before an operation of $T_j$. A schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this graph has no cycle, and any topological order of the graph is an equivalent serial schedule.

steps.title: Schedule $S_1$
steps.body: Items: $x$ has $r_1, r_2, w_1$; $y$ has $r_1, r_2, w_2$. On $y$, $r_1(y)$ comes before $w_2(y)$: $T_1\to T_2$. On $x$, $r_2(x)$ comes before $w_1(x)$: $T_2\to T_1$. The two edges form a cycle, so $S_1$ is not conflict serializable.

steps.title: Schedule $S_2$
steps.body: On $x$, $r_2(x)$ before $w_1(x)$: $T_2\to T_1$. On $y$, $w_2(y)$ before $r_1(y)$: $T_2\to T_1$. Every edge points the same way, so there is no cycle, and $S_2$ is equivalent to the serial schedule $T_2$ then $T_1$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: $S_1$ not serializable, $S_2$ serializable: option B.

shortcut.body: Only two transactions, so look for a conflicting pair in each direction. In S1, T1 reads y before T2 writes it while T2 reads x before T1 writes it: both directions. In S2, T1 acts last on both items. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Reversing the verdicts by reading the schedule start: $r_1(x)$ first suggests T1 first. The schedule must be tested against the whole graph.
Missing the $r_1(y)$ versus $w_2(y)$ conflict in $S_1$ because both transactions read $y$ early. The write comes later and still conflicts with the earlier read of the other transaction.
Treating $r_1(x)$ before $r_2(x)$ as a conflict. Two reads never conflict.

recognize.clues: Two named schedules over $r_i$ and $w_i$ of the same two transactions, and a question about whether each is conflict serializable, call for a precedence graph per schedule.
recognize.contrast: View serializability would also allow some schedules with a cycle. The question says conflict serializable, so a cycle is decisive and no blind-write exception applies.

check.body: For $S_1$, argue by contradiction. Any equivalent serial order needs $T_1$ before $T_2$ because $r_1(y)$ precedes $w_2(y)$, and $T_2$ before $T_1$ because $r_2(x)$ precedes $w_1(x)$. Both cannot hold. For $S_2$, write the serial schedule $T_2$ then $T_1$ and compare: $r_2(x)$ before $w_1(x)$ and $w_2(y)$ before $r_1(y)$ both match.

questions.stem:
Suppose a database system crashes again while recovering from a previous crash. Assume checkpointing is not done by the database either during the transactions or during recovery.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again.
The system cannot recover any further.
All the transactions that are already undone and redone will not be recovered again.

steps.title: How log-based recovery works
steps.body: The DBMS writes every update to a **log** on stable storage before changing the database. After a crash, recovery scans the log and builds two lists: transactions that committed, which are **redone** (their writes are applied again), and transactions that never committed, which are **undone** (their writes are rolled back using old values). Both operations are **idempotent**: doing them twice leaves the same result as doing them once.

steps.title: A crash during recovery
steps.body: Recovery only reads the log and sets data values; it does not change which transactions had committed. With no checkpoint, the scan starts from the same place and sees the same log, so it produces the same undo list and redo list. Statement A is true.

steps.title: Why the others fail
steps.body: B is false: recovery can always be restarted, as idempotence guarantees. C is false: the system does not remember what the interrupted recovery already finished, so the same transactions are undone and redone again. D is false: replaying the log gives the same consistent state however many times it runs.

shortcut.body: Recovery is restartable and idempotent, so the second attempt just repeats the first with the same lists. Choose A and reject any option saying recovery fails, or skips work already done. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Assuming progress is remembered. Without checkpoints the log offers no marker of what recovery completed, so everything is redone or undone again, harmlessly.
Believing that a second crash corrupts the log. The log is on stable storage and recovery never writes to it in a way that blocks a retry.
Thinking half-applied redo leaves inconsistency. Redo writes complete values, so repeating it converges to the same state.

recognize.clues: "Crashes again while recovering" and "checkpointing is not done" fix the scenario to restarting redo and undo from the same log with no marker of progress.
recognize.contrast: With checkpoints, recovery could begin at the last checkpoint, so the lists might differ. The question removes that option, which is why the lists stay the same.

check.body: Substitute concrete values. If the log says item $A$ goes from 10 to 20 and $T$ committed, redo writes $A=20$; after a crash and a second redo, $A$ is still 20. If $T$ never committed, undo writes $A=10$ both times. Repeating either step cannot change the outcome because each writes a fixed value, not an increment.

questions.stem:
Consider the following two statements about database transaction schedules:

I. Strict two-phase locking protocol generates conflict serializable schedules that are also recoverable.
II. Timestamp-ordering concurrency control protocol with Thomas' Write Rule can generate view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?

steps.title: The terms
steps.body: **Two-phase locking (2PL)**: a transaction never takes a lock after releasing one. **Strict 2PL**: additionally it holds all its write locks until it commits or aborts. A schedule is **recoverable** when each transaction commits after every transaction it read from. **View serializable**: equivalent to a serial schedule in who reads whose write and who writes last; every conflict serializable schedule is view serializable, but not the other way round (the extra ones contain blind writes). **Thomas' Write Rule**: under timestamp ordering, a write that arrives too late is simply skipped, since a newer write has already replaced it.

steps.title: Statement I
steps.body: Any 2PL schedule is conflict serializable (order by lock points). Under strict 2PL nobody can read or overwrite an uncommitted write, so a reader always commits after the writer: schedules are strict, hence cascadeless and recoverable. I is true.

steps.title: Statement II
steps.body: Skipping an obsolete write can produce a schedule whose conflicts form a cycle but whose reads and final writes match a serial schedule. For example with timestamps $TS(T_1)<TS(T_2)<TS(T_3)$: $r_1(A)\,w_2(A)\,w_1(A)\,w_3(A)$. The late $w_1(A)$ is dropped under Thomas' rule, and the result is view equivalent to $T_1T_2T_3$. As submitted, though, $r_1(A)$ before $w_2(A)$ and $w_2(A)$ before $w_1(A)$ give edges both ways between $T_1$ and $T_2$, so the schedule is not conflict serializable. II is true.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Both are true: option C.

shortcut.body: Recall: strict 2PL gives conflict serializable and strict (so recoverable); Thomas' rule is the standard source of view-but-not-conflict serializable schedules. Two textbook facts, about 1 minute.

traps.text: Accepting I but rejecting II because the timestamp protocol is "serializable" and so assumed to be conflict serializable. Thomas' rule goes beyond basic timestamp ordering.
Doubting I because plain 2PL is not recoverable. The statement is about strict 2PL, which is.
Rejecting both from half-remembered exceptions; each statement states a standard theorem.

recognize.clues: Statement I names "strict two-phase locking" with "recoverable", and statement II names "Thomas' Write Rule" with "view serializable ... not conflict serializable". Each is a named protocol property to check.
recognize.contrast: Basic timestamp ordering without the skip rule yields only conflict serializable schedules. The extra view-serializable schedules appear only when late writes are dropped, which is what separates Thomas' rule from plain timestamp ordering.

check.body: Check I by the lock rules: a transaction that wants to read an item written by an uncommitted $T_i$ needs a shared lock, but $T_i$ still holds the exclusive lock until it commits, so the reader waits and commits later. Every reads-from pair therefore has the writer committing first, which is recoverability. Check II by the timestamp tests: when $w_1(A)$ arrives, $W\text{-}TS(A)=TS(T_2)$ is larger than $TS(T_1)$, so basic timestamp ordering would abort $T_1$; $R\text{-}TS(A)=TS(T_1)$ is not larger than $TS(T_1)$, so Thomas' rule only skips the write and no abort is needed. That skip is exactly what lets this schedule through despite its conflict cycle.

questions.stem:
Two transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$ are given as
$T_1$: $r_1(X)\,w_1(X)\,r_1(Y)\,w_1(Y)$
$T_2$: $r_2(Y)\,w_2(Y)\,r_2(Z)\,w_2(Z)$
where $r_i(V)$ denotes a read operation by transaction $T_i$ on a variable $V$ and $w_i(V)$ denotes a write operation by transaction $T_i$ on a variable $V$. The total number of conflict serializable schedules that can be formed by $T_1$ and $T_2$ is ______

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: A **schedule** is one interleaving of the operations of several transactions, each transaction keeping its own order. Two operations **conflict** when they come from different transactions, touch the same data item, and at least one is a write: read-write, write-read and write-write. Swapping two adjacent operations that do not conflict changes nothing; swapping two that conflict can change what a transaction reads or what the database ends up holding. Two schedules are **conflict equivalent** when every conflicting pair appears in the same order in both. The **precedence graph** has one node per transaction and an edge $T_i \to T_j$ whenever an operation of $T_i$ conflicts with and comes before an operation of $T_j$. A schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this graph has no cycle, and any topological order of the graph is an equivalent serial schedule. Two schedules with the same operations may differ only in interleaving, and each transaction keeps its internal order.

steps.title: Only item Y can conflict
steps.body: X appears only in $T_1$ and Z only in $T_2$, so only the Y operations create edges: $r_1(Y), w_1(Y)$ against $r_2(Y), w_2(Y)$. There are two transactions, so a cycle needs edges in both directions. The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when all conflicting Y pairs point the same way: all of $T_1$'s Y operations before $T_2$'s ($T_1\to T_2$), or all of $T_2$'s before $T_1$'s.

steps.title: Case $T_1\to T_2$
steps.body: We need $w_1(Y)$, the last operation of $T_1$, before $r_2(Y)$, the first of $T_2$. That forces all of $T_1$ before all of $T_2$: exactly 1 schedule.

steps.title: Case $T_2\to T_1$
steps.body: We need $w_2(Y)$ before $r_1(Y)$. Write $T_1=a\,b\,c\,d$ (with $c=r_1(Y)$) and $T_2=p\,q\,r\,s$ (with $q=w_2(Y)$). Count the schedules with $q$ before $c$ by complement: the total is $\binom{8}{4}=70$. Schedules with $c$ before $q$: if $d$ is also before $q$, all of $T_1$ precedes $q$ and $p$ has 5 slots, giving 5; if $d$ is after $q$, then $a,b,c$ interleave with $p$ in 4 ways before $q$, and $d$ with $r,s$ after $q$ in 3 ways, giving 12. So 17 schedules have $c$ before $q$, and $70-17=53$ have $q$ before $c$.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: The two cases cannot overlap, because $T_1\to T_2$ and $T_2\to T_1$ are exclusive. The total is $1+53=54$.

shortcut.body: Total interleavings are 70. Non-serializable ones need Y operations in both orders; the bad count is 16, so the answer is $70-16=54$. Count the bad ones as the 17 schedules with $c$ before $q$ minus the single serial one. About 3 minutes; the case split is the safest route.

traps.text: Answering 70, the number of all interleavings, or 2, the number of serial schedules. Many interleavings are equivalent to a serial one.
Answering 53 or 1 by counting only one direction of the Y order. Both $T_1\to T_2$ and $T_2\to T_1$ count.
Treating $r_1(Y)$ and $r_2(Y)$ as a conflict and halving the count. Two reads never conflict.

recognize.clues: "The total number of conflict serializable schedules that can be formed" by two short transactions asks for a count over interleavings, with a serializability test applied to each.
recognize.contrast: Counting all interleavings gives $\binom{8}{4}$, and counting serial schedules gives 2. The required number lies between them, so conflicts must be applied rather than either shortcut.

check.body: Recount the $T_2\to T_1$ case as lattice paths from $(0,0)$ to $(4,4)$, where $i$ and $j$ count operations done by $T_1$ and $T_2$. Need $w_2(Y)$, the second step of $T_2$, before $r_1(Y)$, the third of $T_1$. Reaching $j=2$ at $i=0,1,2$ gives $1\cdot15+2\cdot10+3\cdot6=53$. Add the one schedule with $T_1$ wholly first to get 54.

questions.stem:
In a database system, unique timestamps are assigned to each transaction using Lamport's logical clock. Let $TS(T_1)$ and $TS(T_2)$ be the timestamps of transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively. Besides, $T_1$ holds a lock on the resource $R$, and $T_2$ has requested a conflicting lock on the same resource $R$. The following algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks in the database system assuming that a killed transaction is restarted with the same timestamp.

if $TS(T_2) < TS(T_1)$ then $T_1$ is killed else $T_2$ waits.

Assume any transaction that is not killed terminates eventually. Which of the following is TRUE about the database system that uses the above algorithm to prevent deadlocks?
options: The database system is both deadlock-free and starvation-free.
The database system is deadlock-free, but not starvation-free.
The database system is starvation-free, but not deadlock-free.
The database system is neither deadlock-free nor starvation-free.

solutionDiagram.alt: Four transactions on a line from oldest to youngest with arrows from each younger transaction to an older one it waits for; arrows only go left.

steps.title: Deadlock and starvation
steps.body: A **deadlock** is a cycle of transactions each waiting for a lock held by the next. **Starvation** is a transaction that is killed or made to wait again and again and never finishes. A **timestamp** is a unique age label: smaller means older. The rule here is the **wound-wait** scheme: if the requester is older than the holder, the holder is killed (wounded); if the requester is younger, it waits.

steps.title: Deadlock-free
steps.body: A transaction waits only when the requester is younger than the holder, so every waits-for edge goes from a larger timestamp to a smaller one. Following edges, timestamps strictly decrease, so you can never return to where you started. No cycle, no deadlock.
steps.tex: T_i \text{ waits for } T_j \Rightarrow TS(T_i) > TS(T_j)

steps.title: Starvation-free
steps.body: A killed transaction restarts with the same timestamp, so its age is never reset. Younger ones that arrive later cannot kill it; only older ones can. The oldest transaction in the system is never killed and, by the stated assumption, finishes. Then the next oldest becomes oldest, and so on, so every transaction eventually finishes.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Both properties hold: option A.

shortcut.body: Recognise wound-wait, and note that the restart keeps the old timestamp: that is the clause that kills starvation. Wound-wait with preserved timestamps is the textbook deadlock-free, starvation-free scheme. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Saying starvation can occur because the same transaction may be killed repeatedly. Each restart keeps its old timestamp, so it only gets relatively older.
Claiming waiting can still cycle. Waits only run from younger to older, so no cycle can close.
Mixing up this rule with schemes where a restarted transaction gets a fresh, larger timestamp; that variant can starve.

recognize.clues: An age-based rule on lock requests ("if $TS(T_2) < TS(T_1)$ then kill, else wait") with restart under the same timestamp is a deadlock-prevention scheme, and the question asks about deadlock and starvation.
recognize.contrast: Deadlock detection builds a wait-for graph and breaks cycles after they form. Prevention schemes such as this one use timestamps so a cycle can never form.

check.body: Try to build a cycle with three transactions and see it fail: a cycle $T_a\to T_b\to T_c\to T_a$ would need $TS(T_a)>TS(T_b)>TS(T_c)>TS(T_a)$, which is impossible. For starvation, consider the oldest transaction $O$. Every time it requests a lock held by another, $TS(O)$ is smaller, so the holder is killed and $O$ never waits or dies.
